list.listitem: Isolate any traveler with acute febrile illness and hemorrhagic manifestations who is returning from an endemic area and obtain blood for virus isolation and serology. C
Administer ribavirin to patients with severe hemorrhagic fever until viral etiology has been determined. Continue ribavirin in patients with proven Lassa fever infection. B
Vaccinate any traveler going to areas endemic for yellow fever at least 10 days prior to travel date. A

background.definition: Viral febrile syndrome is caused by 4 families of RNA viruses: Flaviridae, Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Filoviridae. The syndrome is characterized by fever, flulike illness, gastroenteritis, progression to prostration, microvessel or small vessel vascular damage, and hemorrhage.

list.listitem: Dengue fever: 0.007% in nonexposed patients and 1% in previously exposed patients
Yellow fever: 1 to 2.4 cases/1000 persons in Africa; 10-fold lower incidence in the United States
Lassa fever: 10% to 20% infection rate
Hantavirus: dozens of cases per year in the United States
Rift Valley fever: hundreds of cases per year in sub-Saharan Africa
Ebola/Marburg: occur in outbreaks

In an economic analysis in 8 countries in the Americas and Asia, the estimated cost of Dengue fever was I$587 million (international dollars). Mean costs were I$514 and I$1394 for an ambulatory and hospitalized case, respectively.
Dengue fever mortality: 10% to 15% in nonhospitalized cases; 1% in hospitalized cases
Yellow fever mortality: 20% to 50% in hospitalized severe cases
Lassa fever mortality: 76% for untreated cases, 2% to 15% for ribavirin-treated cases
Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) mortality: 40% to 50%, even with supportive care
Rift Valley fever mortality: 50%, even with supportive care
Ebola/Marburg fever mortality: 74%, even with supportive care
Flaviridae: yellow fever, Dengue (types 1-4), Omsk hemorrhagic fever
Arenaviridae: Lassa, Junin, Machupo, Guanarito
Bunyaviridae: Hantaan, Rift Valley fever, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, Sin Nombre
Filoviridae: Marburg, Ebola
Dengue fever: increased platelet destruction and antiplatelet antibodies; increased vascular permeability due to antibody-mediated enhancement of secondary infection.
Yellow fever: increased pro-inflammatory cytokines; organ damage due to viral invasion in heart, kidney, liver
Lassa fever: microvascular leak causing shock and multiorgan dysfunction
Hantavirus: severe pulmonary edema due to increased vascular permeability
Rift Valley fever: decreased platelets due to disseminated intravascular coagulation; myocardial necrosis
Ebola/Marburg: cardiogenic shock due to myocarditis; bleeding and pulmonary edema

Yellow fever primary prevention: A live-attenuated virus (17D strain) vaccine is given as a single 0.5 mL SC injection. It induces neutralizing antibodies in 90% of recipients within 10 days and 99% of recipients within 30 days of administration. Protection is lifelong. Healthy individuals (aged 9 months or older) traveling to areas of high exposure should receive the vaccine. The vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy (potential risk of congenital infection) and immunosuppressed individuals (potential risk of infection). A
Dengue fever primary prevention: An effective vaccine has not yet been developed despite extensive research.
Transmission prevention: (1) Avoid mosquito bites with repellent and bed nets (Dengue fever, Yellow fever, and Rift Valley fever); and (2) avoid human-rodent contact (Lassa fever and HPS). C

Ebola prevention: Ebola vaccine is well tolerated and shows a robust immune response in a randomized trial with 2800 participants. Observational studies show Ebola vaccine also appears to reduce the risk of death.
Suspect a hemorrhagic fever syndrome in any traveler with fever and hemorrhagic symptoms after returning from an endemic area and obtain blood for virus isolation and serology. C
Viral isolation by culture, viral antigen ELISA or IgM ELISA or immunofluorescent antibodies. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Skin rash, travel to endemic area

list.listitem: Dengue fever: Sudden onset of fever and flulike illness. Fever lasts 5 to 7 days. Flushed face, petechial/maculopapular rash for 1 to 2 days during defervescence (50% of patients).

Yellow fever: Mild form causes acute febrile illness with sudden onset of severe headaches, leg pain, conjunctival injection, and tachycardia. The severe form follows a 1-day remission of the mild form, characterized by bradycardia, hypotension, jaundice, and bleeding.

Lassa fever: Prostration and shock. Hemorrhage and neurologic signs are less frequent than with other hemorrhagic fevers. Common symptoms are retrosternal chest pain (76%), sore throat (60%), back pain (62%), cough (62%), and abdominal pain (50%). The presence of fever, pharyngitis, retrosternal pain, and proteinuria predicted 70% of laboratory-confirmed Lassa fever.

HPS: Prodromal stage (3-5 days) consisting of abrupt onset of fever, myalgia/malaise, anorexia and headache, and no cough. This is followed by the onset of pulmonary edema with dyspnea, cough, hypotension, fever, and arterial desaturation. Hypoxemia, due to pulmonary edema, and shock, due to microvascular leak, follow.

Rift Valley fever: Sudden onset of fever lasting 4 days with myalgias, malaise, retro-orbital pain, and anorexia. In a minority of patients, symptoms return after 2 to 3 days with maculopapular rash. Progression in 50% of patients occurs with disseminated intravascular coagulation, renal failure, hepatitis, and GI bleeding. Death may occur in 3 to 6 days. However, most patients recover; convalescence lasts 2 to 3 weeks. Complications include encephalitis, optic neuropathy, and hepatitis.

Ebola or Marburg hemorrhagic fevers: Fever and severe constitutional symptoms, conjunctival injection, maculopapular rash, asthenia, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and prostration. Bleeding diathesis, anuria, and tachypnea herald death approximately 10 days after onset of symptoms. Complications among survivors include severe cachexia, arthralgias, orchitis, hearing loss, uveitis, encephalopathy, and retinitis. In the 2014 Ebola outbreak hemorrhagic symptoms were uncommon. The most common signs and symptoms were fever, headache, weakness, dizziness, and diarrhea. Other common symptoms were abdominal pain, sore throat, vomiting, and conjunctivitis.,

Perform the following diagnostic tests on patients with suspected viral hemorrhagic fever: CBC with differential, electrolytes, creatinine and BUN, liver injury tests, and coagulation tests (prothrombin time/partial thromboplastin time). Laboratory features of specific syndromes are listed below. Dengue fever: severe thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, increased hepatic aminotransferases. Yellow fever: moderate thrombocytopenia, increased hepatic aminotransferases and bilirubin. Lassa fever: mild thrombocytopenia. HPS: moderate thrombocytopenia, marked hypoxemia. Rift Valley fever: severe thrombocytopenia and moderate hyperbilirubinemia. Ebola or Marburg hemorrhagic fever: In the 2014 Ebola outbreak fatal disease was associated with higher BUN and creatiine and elevated transaminases. In earlier outbreaks severe thrombocytopenia and moderate hyperbilirubinemia was seen.

For early diagnosis of Dengue fever, a study of direct immunofluorescence staining for the presence of dengue viral antigen in peripheral blood mononuclear cells demonstrated a sensitivity of 93.8% (95% CI, 88.8%-98.9%) and a specificity of 100% in patients in the febrile stage. Work is also in progress on a dengue NS1 antigen strip for early diagnosis.
A real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is also being developed for Rift Valley fever.
Consider hemorrhagic fever syndrome in any traveler returning from an endemic area with fever and hemorrhagic manifestations of less than 3 weeks' duration.
The clinical findings vary for each type of hemorrhagic fever virus. Individual syndromes are difficult to diagnose without virologic testing.
In the 2014 Ebola outbreak the average time from onset of symptoms to presentation was 5.7 days. The incubation period is estimated at 6 to 12 days.
Treatment is primarily supportive. B
Ribavirin is indicated for severe cases of Lassa fever. B
Ribavirin has been used in patients with Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever and may be useful for Rift Valley fever. C

Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment of hemorrhagic fevers. It consists of careful maintenance of fluid and electrolyte balance, circulatory volume, and blood pressure. Consider early vasopressor use to avoid fluid overload and pulmonary edema in appropriate cases (HPS). Mechanical ventilation, dialysis, and antiseizure medication may be needed.

Ebola prevention: A randomized trial comparing the triple monoclonal antibody ZMapp + standard care with ZMapp (three 50 mg/kg IV infusions every 3 days) in 72 patients found a non-significant trend in favor of ZMapp (22% mortality vs 37% mortality, mortality reduction 15%, 95% CI -36% to 7%).

Ribavirin is active in vitro and in vivo against Arenaviridae and Bunyaviridae, but not against Filoviridae or Flaviviridae. Ribavirin given within the first 6 days of fever reduces mortality in severe Lassa fever (from 76% to 9%). It does not penetrate the blood-brain barrier, so is not useful to treat encephalitis symptoms. It has been used in Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever and may be useful in Rift Valley fever.
The single monoclonal antibody MAb114 and the drug REGN-EB3 are both more effective than ZMapp or remdesivir for Ebola virus.
Hemolytic anemia is a potential adverse effect of ribavirin in this setting; in one study, it occurred in 76.5% of 38 individuals treated for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.
Dosage: A 30 mg/kg IV loading dose given once, followed by 15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 4 days, followed by 8 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 6 days.

In one study of patients with Dengue fever and thrombocytopenia, infusion of 600 mL of fresh frozen plasma contributed to a significant increase in platelet count in the first 12 hours, but not thereafter.
In another study, use of high-dose IV immunoglobulin was not effective for treatment of severe thrombocytopenia.
Steroids were harmful when tested for Dengue fever and should not be used.
Please refer to for treatment for each specific viral hemorrhagic fever.

In a RCT, a community-based environmental management embedded in a routine control program (entomological surveillance, source reduction, selective adulticiding, and health education) was more effective than the control program alone at reducing levels of Aedes infestation, the vector of dengue.
In the United States, all patients with suspected viral hemorrhagic fever should be hospitalized and isolated.

In endemic areas, patients with Dengue fever with shock (lethargy, circumoral cyanosis, hypotension, and narrowing of pulse pressure to <20 mmHg) or a sudden increase of hematocrit levels should be hospitalized. All patients with yellow fever should be hospitalized.

In a study of Dengue fever (N = 1973 and 6% with hemorrhagic disease), a combination of clinical bleeding, serum urea, and serum total protein had a sensitivity of 1.00, specificity of 0.46, positive predictive value of 7.5%, and negative predictive value of 100% for hemorrhagic disease; use of these factors might prevent hospitalization for almost 44% of mild Dengue fever cases.
Prognosis and mortality depend on the specific virus causing hemorrhagic fever syndrome. For Dengue fever and yellow fever, hemoconcentration carries a poor prognosis. C
Lassa fever: Consider using ribavirin in pregnant women with proven severe disease.

Children are less likely to present with Dengue hemorrhagic fever than adults since they are less likely to have been previously infected with a different Dengue virus prior to the initial presentation.
The use of ribavirin is indicated in cases of severe disease.
